title: Ashtpadi 6, salok: the thieves leave
hookLine: lust, anger, greed and attachment go, and pride too, by grace

lines: LIVING IN THE HOUSE OF THE BODY.
cards: You may remember them from last year: the five thieves. Kaam, lust. Krodh, anger.
Lobh, greed. Moh, attachment. Ahankaar, pride.

Elsewhere the Guru Granth Sahib pictures five thieves living inside the body, quietly carrying off whatever is valuable. Last year they came as a list. Ashtpadi six opens by naming them again, all five, in a single line.
But this time the salok isn't describing the thieves. It's asking for something, and what it asks for is the surprise.

teach.b: The salok's first line lists them: kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, and then ahanmev, pride, the sense of I alone, I myself. And it asks that they be destroyed, that they go.
You might expect the second line to give a method: five steps, a discipline for each thief. Instead it says: Nanak has come to God's sanctuary; bless me with Your grace, O divine Guru.
The word for sanctuary is saranaagatee, coming for refuge, the way someone being chased runs to a protected house.
The word for grace is prasaad, a gift freely given. So the salok's answer to the five thieves isn't a fight in the dark. It's a door, and a request: run to the safe house, and ask.
That doesn't mean Sikhs sit back and do nothing. Elsewhere the Gurus speak of effort and of an honest, disciplined life. But this salok says something about where the change finally comes from.
Pride can't be beaten by more pride, even pride in being humble. Anger can't be shouted down.
The house is cleared by grace, coming in from outside. And that sets up all of ashtpadi six.
Over the next days it repeats one phrase again and again: jih prasaad, by whose grace.

how: Sikhs name kaam, krodh, lobh, moh and ahankaar as the five thieves, and in this salok of Sukhmani Sahib the request is for the Guru's grace against them.

o: coming for refuge, running to a safe house
a fast kept to drive out the five thieves
a long night of singing in the gurdwara

games.q: the sixth salok — tap the pairs.

s: the salok gives a five-step method for beating each thief
it asks for grace from the Guru's sanctuary.
the salok names pride along with lust, anger, greed and attachment
Sikh teaching says effort and discipline don't matter
the Gurus speak of effort and an honest life; this salok says where the change finally comes from.

games.q: five thieves are in the house. in the salok, what does Nanak do?
o: fight each one alone in the dark.
run to God's sanctuary and ask for grace.
games.why: prabh saranaagatee: Nanak comes to God's sanctuary and asks the divine Guru for prasaad.

practice: Without judging yourself, let one of the five come to mind, the one you know best, lust, anger, greed, clinging or pride, and just name it.

Breathe in slowly, as if the door of the house were opening, and as you breathe out, picture that thief walking out through it; you're not chasing it, only making room, and if you pray, ask for grace in your own way.

wordCard.voice: Saranaagatee, coming for refuge: ashtpadi six's salok names the five thieves, and asks for grace, prasaad, from the sanctuary of the Guru.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: saranaagatee, coming to someone's protection for refuge; Nanak's answer to the five thieves.

carryVoice: Your line: grace clears the house. Five thieves, and one open door to the sanctuary. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sorath M3, Ang 600 (five thieves within the body)
